The hire, ask, queue, issue and meeting windows show it on one line; click **✏️ Edit** there to pick **Claude Code**, **OpenCode**, **Codex**, **Grok**, **Muse**, **DeepSeek Harness**, **Pi** or **Cursor**, a model and an effort for just that worker or task, and **↺ Use the default** to go back. Board agents and tasks the Queue agent adds, which nobody picks for, start on the default too. Existing workers keep their provider when prompted or resumed, and queued tasks keep their choice when retried or restored after a restart.\n\nEvery harness takes both a **Model** and an **Effort**, each optional: leave one on **Default** and the harness uses its own settings.\n\n| Harness | Model | Effort |\n| --- | --- | --- |\n| Claude Code | Fable 5.1, Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5 or Haiku 4.5 (`--model`) | `--effort` |\n| OpenCode | a `provider/model`, typed or picked from the suggestions `opencode models` gives (`--model`) | the model's variant |\n| Codex | one of the models `codex debug models` lists (`--model`) | `-c model_reasoning_effort` |\n| Grok | one of the models `grok models` lists (`--model`) | `--effort` |\n| Muse | a model id, typed (`--model`) | `--reasoning-effort` |\n| DeepSeek Harness | a model id from its catalog, typed | its `reasoning_effort` option |\n| Pi | a model name or `provider/model`, typed (`--model`) | **Thinking** (`--thinking`) |\n\nThe efforts are low, medium, high, extra high and max. Where a harness's own catalog says which of them a model supports (Codex and OpenCode do), the ones it doesn't are greyed out once that model is picked. A harness whose models can't be listed (its CLI isn't installed, or isn't signed in) still takes a model id typed in. A **Custom** `--agent` is run as it is, so it has neither field: set its model and effort in `--agent-args`.\n\nWhat's picked shows next to the worker everywhere it's named (the Workers panel, its task card, its terminal's title, the queue), by the model's name rather than its family: **Opus 5.5**, not \"Opus\". For Claude Code that name comes from the session itself once the worker has spoken, so a worker left on Default says which model the default is, and one switched with `/model` in its terminal says the new one.\n\nFor OpenCode, the **Model** field selects the initial model for a new worker or queue task. Suggestions come from `opencode models`; you can also enter a `provider/model` ID. Leave it empty to use your OpenCode settings (including configured CLI arguments). An explicit choice overrides configured model arguments for that launch and stays with a queued task when retried. **Effort** is what OpenCode calls the model's *variant*. Its TUI has no flag for one, and sends each message at the variant it remembers for the model from whichever session used it last, so the office's plugin puts the worker's first message on the effort picked for it; the TUI carries on from that message, and `Ctrl+T` in the terminal still changes it. An effort the model has no variant for changes nothing.\n\n**Pi** is available in the worker picker, queued tasks, meetings, and the office default. Install and sign in to the Pi coding-agent CLI on the machine running the office (`npm install -g @earendil-works/pi-coding-agent`, then `pi` and `/login`). The integration targets Pi 0.87.1 or later, using its `agent_settled` and UI prompt extension events. Choose Pi when hiring, or start the office with `--agent pi`. Windows npm `.cmd` launchers are supported.\n\nPi keeps its own login, settings, packages, and extensions. The office adds a CLI-loaded extension to report session, working, tool, waiting-for-input, and completion events; it does not edit your Pi configuration. Each worker's sessions live under `.agent-office/pi-sessions/<worker-id>`, and **R** resumes that worker's session. The optional **Model** field accepts a model name or `provider/model`; **Thinking** offers low, medium, high, xhigh, and max. Leave either on Default to use Pi settings or configured `--agent-args` (including `--thinking off` or `minimal`). Cost and token metrics remain in Pi's terminal and are not included in the office's Claude budget.\n\nFor Claude Code, the **Model** and **Effort** fields pick `--model` (`fable`, `opus`, `sonnet` or `haiku`, listed by the model each alias stands for: Fable 5.1, Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, Haiku 4.5) and `--effort` (low, medium, high, extra high or max) for that worker or queue task, overriding whatever `--agent-args` set office-wide. Leave either on **Default** to use the office's configured value. The choice stays with a worker across resumes and with a queued task when retried, and shows up next to the worker in the Workers panel and on its task card so you can tell at a glance who's on what — and the per-worker cost there reflects the actual model used.\n\nIn an open OpenCode terminal, **Models** opens the native model picker using the default `Ctrl+X M` shortcut. Select a model there to change the active worker without restarting it or losing a draft. If you customized that binding, use your configured shortcut or `/models` inside the terminal. Resuming a saved session lets OpenCode restore its current model instead of forcing the initial Office selection again.\n\nClaude Code remains the default. To default to OpenCode:\n\n```bash\nagent-office /path/to/project --agent opencode\n```\n\n`--agent-args` applies only to the provider configured by `--agent`; choosing another provider uses its normal command and settings. OpenCode model flags therefore never reach Claude Code, and vice versa. Grok's `--model` / `--effort` and Muse's `--model` / `--reasoning-effort` for a worker likewise stay with that provider. An arbitrary `--agent` executable remains available as **Custom**, with whatever model and effort its `--agent-args` give it.\n\nOpenCode receives prompts through `--prompt` and resumes its saved session through `--session`. The office adds a local event plugin through `OPENCODE_CONFIG_CONTENT`, preserving existing inline JSON settings and plugin entries. Inline settings must be a JSON object; configuration files continue to use OpenCode's own loader. The office does not edit your OpenCode configuration files or bypass permission prompts. The bridge reports worker status to a loopback endpoint authenticated by a per-worker token. OpenCode, Codex, Grok, Muse, DeepSeek Harness, Pi and the Cursor CLI must be installed separately on servers set up with `deploy/provision.sh` (or the AWS script), which installs Claude Code only.\n\nGrok uses its interactive CLI with `--no-alt-screen`, a per-office `GROK_HOME` for session and hook files (your grok.com login is still read from `~/.grok/auth.json`; 🔐 Your sign-ins is Claude and GitHub), and resumes through `grok --resume <session-id>`. Set it as the default with `--agent grok`. The office writes command hooks into that isolated home so a worker can report status without editing `~/.grok/hooks`. `--trust` skips Grok's folder-trust prompt for the project the desk is already in; native permission prompts still appear in the terminal. The **Model** and **Effort** fields pick `--model` and `--effort` for that worker or queue task. Leave either on **Default** to use your Grok settings. Token spend stays in the worker terminal; the office does not meter grok.com billing.\n\nMuse uses its interactive CLI with `--trust-workspace`, a per-office XDG tree under the floor's `.agent-office/muse-home` (your login is linked from `~/.config/muse/auth.json`; 🔐 Your sign-ins is Claude and GitHub), and resumes through `muse resume <session-id>`. Set it as the default with `--agent muse`. The office writes command hooks into that isolated home so a worker can report status without editing `~/.config/muse`. `--trust-workspace` skips Muse's folder-trust prompt for the project the desk is already in; native permission prompts still appear in the terminal. The **Model** and **Effort** fields pick `--model` and `--reasoning-effort` for that worker or queue task. Leave either blank / on **Default** to use your Muse settings. A follow-up prompt on resume is pasted into the TUI after SessionStart, because `muse resume` does not take a prompt on argv. Token spend stays in the worker terminal; the office does not meter Muse billing.\n\nDeepSeek Harness has no interactive terminal, so the office drives it over its **ACP profile** (`dsh --profile acp`, newline-delimited JSON-RPC on stdio) instead of a PTY. The laptop still shows a terminal, but it is the transcript the office renders from ACP: committed messages, thoughts, tool calls and their outcomes, and what is in the context window. Type a line and press **Enter** to send it as one prompt; **Esc** or **Ctrl+C** cancels the turn. There are no slash-commands (`/compact` and friends are not on the ACP surface), and the terminal does not resize the agent. Status comes from the ACP session itself: `session/prompt` in flight is *working*, an outstanding `session/request_permission` is *needs input*, and a settled turn is *done*, with no hooks to install or trust.\n\nThe **Model** field names a model from its catalog: type the model id (`deepseek-v4-pro`) and the office matches it against the options the session advertises, then applies it with `session/set_config_option`. The **Effort** field works the same way, on DSH's own ladder (`low`, `high`, `max`): the office's *Medium* and *High* both land on `high`, and *Extra high* and *Max* on `max`. Leave either empty for the profile's default. A saved choice the harness no longer offers is reported in the terminal and the profile default is used instead.\n\nThe transcript is styled after the harness's own chat, in its colors (its `--dsw-alias-*` dark-theme tokens) and its wording:\n\n- **Reasoning** opens a `✻ Think` block, ruled down the left in the harness's tertiary text color, and closes with a blank line before the answer. It is never italic, matching the chat.\n- **Markdown is rendered**, not printed raw: headings, bold, italic, inline code (on the harness's code background), bullets, quotes, links and fenced code blocks all come out formatted.\n- **A tool call is one row**: its icon, the harness's own title for that tool (`Bash`, `Read`, `Search`, `Edit`, `Write`, `Code`, `Fetch`…), a dot, and the argument it summarizes by (the command, the path, the query), in the chat's secondary/tertiary colors. A finished call is left collapsed the way the chat leaves it, so there is no tick and no second line; a call that **failed** gets a `└` line in the error color with the reason and up to eight lines of its output.\n- **Each turn ends with the chat's process row**: `Worked · 3 tool calls`, or `Stopped` when you cancelled, or `Failed`.\n- **An approval** is the harness's approval card in text: `▲ Waiting for approval` plus `Tool <name> requests privileged execution`, the numbered choices (reject in the error color, allow in the warning's), and the same keys the chat binds: **Enter** allows once, **Esc** rejects, or a number picks any listed choice. Enter only ever means *allow once*: a request that offers only *always* needs its number typed, and a blank line in something you paste is not an Enter. The card shows the full command being approved. The turn genuinely blocks until it is answered, and rejecting does not end the turn.\n\nAnything the harness sends that this surface has no place for (plans, modes, commands) is skipped rather than printed, and escape sequences in model or tool text are stripped so nothing it says can redraw the terminal.\n\nSet it as the default with `--agent dsh`, and choose the profile with `--dsh-profile <name>` (default `acp`, also `AGENT_OFFICE_DSH_PROFILE`). `--agent-args` is passed through ahead of the profile flags when DSH is the configured agent. DSH rewrites its own profile file on every boot, so the user running the office needs write access to `$DSH_HOME` (`~/.dsh`); a read-only home fails the launch before any ACP frame is exchanged. The office writes a per-floor patch (`<project>/.agent-office/dsh-patch.yml`) that points DSH's session persistence at `<project>/.agent-office/dsh-sessions`, so **R** resumes exactly the session that worker started instead of whatever is in your `~/.dsh`. A new hire always starts a session of its own; it never picks up another desk's. Resuming a session restores its log without replaying the old turns. Its ACP session is a child of the office process, so unlike the other providers a DeepSeek Harness worker stops with the office and comes back *offline*, resumable with **R**. Driven over ACP as verified against `dsh 0.1.7-rc.2`; see [dsh-acp-integration.md](dsh-acp-integration.md) for the design.\n\nCursor runs the Cursor CLI's terminal (`cursor-agent`) on the office machine's own Cursor login: `cursor-agent login`, or `CURSOR_API_KEY` in the office's environment (🔐 Your sign-ins is Claude and GitHub; a Cursor worker hired by an account still gets that account's GitHub sign-in for `gh`). Pick **Cursor** when hiring, or set it as the default with `--agent cursor-agent`. A new worker starts with `--trust`, which skips Cursor's folder-trust prompt for the folder the desk is already in, with `--model` when one was picked, and with its prompt. **R** resumes its chat with `cursor-agent --resume=<chat id>` (the id its first hook names), and a follow-up prompt goes on that command line too. The office never passes `--force` or `--yolo`, and drops them from `--agent-args`: Cursor's own permission prompts appear in the terminal. The office-owned worktree is the worker's folder, so Cursor's own `--worktree` is never used.\n\nThe Cursor CLI reads hooks from `~/.cursor/hooks.json` and from `.cursor/hooks.json` in the folder it runs in, and nothing moves either, so the office never touches `~/.cursor` and puts each worker's hook entries in `.cursor/hooks.json` of the worker's own folder (its worktree, or the project itself for a board agent) as it starts. They come out when the worker's process ends, when it's sent home and when the office stops, and the file goes with them when it held nothing else. A file the office made is listed in `.git/info/exclude`, so it never counts as a change of the worker's. A project with a `.cursor/hooks.json` of its own keeps its hooks: the office's entries go in next to them, and the file is put back as it was afterwards, though git shows it as modified while a Cursor worker runs there. One with comments in it is left alone, and a worker there reports no status.\n\nThe entries (`sessionStart`, `beforeSubmitPrompt`, `preToolUse`, `postToolUse`, `postToolUseFailure` and `stop`) report to a loopback endpoint with a per-worker token, and pass on only the chat id, your prompt and the tool's name: never the assistant's messages, tool input or output. A subagent's events are ignored. They answer Cursor with no decision of their own. Cursor has no hook for a permission prompt, so a worker waiting on one shows as *working*, with the tool it wants to run, until you answer it in its terminal. A worker on a machine where Cursor isn't signed in is flagged as needing you, and its terminal is where you log in. The **Model** field takes a Cursor model id, with suggestions from `cursor-agent models` when the CLI is signed in; leave it empty to use your Cursor settings. Cursor has no separate effort flag: a parameterized model takes it in brackets, as in `claude-opus-4-8[effort=high]`. Usage and cost stay in Cursor's terminal and your Cursor account; the office doesn't meter them, and the daily budget stays Claude-only. To clone them somewhere else, like `~/Workspace`, an admin picks the **Workspace folder** in ⚙️ Settings → **🏢 Building** (or start with `--projects` or `AGENT_OFFICE_PROJECTS`). Floors you already have stay where they are, and a checkout of the same repository that's already in the new folder is used as it is. The building's map is in `~/agent-office/.agent-office/map.json`, and maps of your own go in `~/agent-office/.agent-office/maps/` (see [Maps](maps.md)). The list of floors is `~/agent-office/.agent-office/floors.json`, and each account's own Claude and GitHub sign-ins are in `~/agent-office/.agent-office/homes/<account>/` (revoking the account deletes them). Each floor keeps its workers, queue, pictures and worktrees in its own checkout's `.agent-office/`.\n\nAlready have a checkout? Pick its repository anyway: a checkout of it that's already where the workspace folder would clone it is used as it is. You can still start the office in a project, `agent-office ~/code/my-project`: that project becomes a floor, and the office keeps its data in `~/code/my-project/.agent-office` as it did before there were floors. [L2]   "content": "# Code layout\n\nBack to the [README](../README.md).\n\nWhere the code lives, and where a new feature's pieces go. The office used to grow by adding to the middle of a few big files: the server's message switch, the page's key handler, its frame loop and its store. Each of those is a registry now, and a feature is a folder of its own plus one line in each list it joins. If a change has you editing the middle of `main.ts`, `server.ts`, the store or `protocol.ts`, it probably belongs somewhere else.\n\nThere are three parts: `src/client` (the page, built by Vite, with three.js), `src/server` (Node) and `src/shared` (types and pure code both use, with no Node imports).\n\n## Client\n\n### `main.ts` and the context\n\n`src/client/main.ts` is the install list: it makes the scene, calls each part's `install…(ctx, …)` in turn, and boots. The order is the order everything registers in (messages, keys, ticks, store topics), and it's kept on purpose, so a new feature's line goes at the end of its group unless it has to come before something.\n\nEvery part gets `ctx`: the `Ctx` type in `core/context.ts`, built by `createCtx` in `core/ctx.ts`. It has the scene, the camera, the player, the socket (`net`), sound, settings, what you're holding, the hint bar, `shake`, and the registries. A feature imports `Ctx` as a type and never imports `main.ts` (a test checks). When a part needs another one, it says which: a small `deps` object of callbacks that `main.ts` passes in (`GongDeps` in `features/gong/index.ts`), or a `Pick` of `Parts` (`core/parts.ts`, every part `main.ts` makes, by name). Parts are only read when something happens, never while installing, so a part can reach one installed after it.\n\n### The registries\n\nThey're in `core/registry.ts`, and each is a field of `ctx`. Every registration hands back an `Off` that takes it out again.\n\n| Registry | What it's for |\n| --- | --- |\n| `ctx.messages` | Server messages. `on(type, fn)` runs `fn` once the store has applied the message (`'before'` as a third argument: before it has); `onAny(fn)` runs on every message. |\n| `ctx.keys` | Key presses. `add(stage, fn)` for the stages before the office's own keys (`guard`, `activity`, `emote`), and `bind({ code, when, run })` for a key of the office's own. |\n| `ctx.ticks` | What runs each frame. `add(phase, fn)`, where the phases run in `TICK_PHASES` order: `pre`, `steer`, `vehicles`, `move`, `moved`, `play`, `me`, `others`, `world`, `env`, `aim`, `hud`, `render`. Within a phase, ticks run in install order. |\n| `ctx.activities` | Something you're in the middle of that takes over the controls (the ladder, the golf tee, a car). It gets keys before the office's own, draws the hint bar, and is stopped by `stopAll(why)` when you start something else. Its place among the others is `ACTIVITY_ORDER` in `core/ctx.ts`. |\n| `ctx.interactions` | What each kind of thing you can use does: `define(kind, { reach, hint, use })`, once per kind. |\n| `ctx.view` | What what you're doing does to your view each frame: something you hold on to, the field of view, covering the screen, or a filter (the drunk vision). |\n| `ctx.windowOpened` | What lets go when a window opens (a shot being wound up, the emote wheel). |\n| `ctx.usables` | Things to use that aren't part of the building and move about (the pictures, the dog, the ball): what each has to use, and what the aim can land on. |\n\n`tests/client-registry.test.ts` pins how each one orders and dispatches.\n\n### Folders\n\n- **`features/<name>/`** is the home of a feature. `index.ts` has its `install<Name>(ctx, deps)`, and beside it is whatever it needs: `controller.ts` (what it does with you), `world.ts` (its 3D things), `sound.ts` (its sound recipes), `ui.ts` and `ui.css` (its window). `features/workers/` is the one without an `index.ts`: its install functions are in `actions.ts` and `views.ts`. `tests/client-structure.test.ts` checks `main.ts` calls every feature's install function once.\n- **`core/`** is the office's own parts that aren't a feature: the renderer and scene (`scene.ts`), the frame loop (`loop.ts`), the building's maps (`worlds.ts`, `maps.ts`), floors and the elevator (`travel.ts`), arriving (`arrival.ts`), where you are (`place.ts`), and the hint bar (`hintbar.ts`, with the pieces every hint is made of in `hint.ts`).\n- **`input/`** is the keyboard (`keyboard.ts`, which hands every press to `ctx.keys`), aiming and clicking (`pointer.ts`), and windows and the game taking turns with both (`focus.ts`).\n- **`state/`** is the store. `store.ts` declares the core fields (who you are, the people, the floors, and the floor you're on with its workers, screens, boards and queue), and `core.ts` keeps them up to date. Everything else is a slice in `state/slices/`: a module that adds its fields and topics to `Store` and `Topics` (`declare module '../store'`), sets where they start (`init`), and says what it takes in from each server message (`on`) and from each floor you arrive on (`enter`). Slices run in the order of `SLICES` in `state/slices/index.ts`, which is the order their topics fire in, so a new one goes at the end. Features follow a topic with `store.on('<topic>', fn)`. What the browser remembers between visits is `persist.ts`.\n- **`ui/`** is the app shell: the HUD, the menu and the windows (settings, the palette, terminals, changes, the queue, and the GitHub windows in `ui/github/`). Each module imports its own stylesheet (`import './palette.css'`), as a feature's `ui.ts` does (`import './ui.css'`).\n- **`world/`** is the engine and the scenery: toon materials and shapes (`toon.ts`), the characters (`world/character/`), the office floor (`world/office/`), the castle (`world/castle/`), the space station (`world/station/`), the scenic loop, the sky and the city. The types they share (what you bump into, what you can use, the seats, `Office`) are in `world/types.ts`.\n- **`sound/`** is the office's sound. `OfficeSound` (`sound/index.ts`, the `ctx.sound` every part uses) is a facade over `AudioCore` (`sound/core.ts`: the audio context, its buses, where your ears are) and the recipes, each in a file of its own, here (`weather.ts`, `steps.ts`) or in its feature's folder (`features/gong/sound.ts`).\n- **`shared/`** (`src/client/shared/`) is what the 3D office and the 2D view at `/lite` both use: the tab title and hiring. The 2D view loads no three.js and nothing from `core/`, `features/`, `input/`, `world/` or `player/`; `tests/client-structure.test.ts` follows `lite.ts`'s imports to check.\n\n### Stylesheets\n\n`style.css` is the 3D office's sheet. It pulls in `styles/base.css` (the colors, the reset, panels, buttons and the window frame, which the 2D view's `lite.css` loads too), `styles/hud.css` and `styles/loading.css`. Every other sheet sits next to its module and comes in with it. A module's sheet loads in no fixed order against `base.css`, so a module rule that overrides a base rule of the same specificity has to be more specific, or live at the end of `base.css` with the others there.\n\n## Server\n\n- **`server.ts`** is the composition root: `startServer` builds the office's context a stage at a time, starts the hook server, opens the floors, and hands the context to the HTTP handler and the WebSocket.\n- **`office/`** is that context (`Ctx` in `office/context.ts`: the building-wide services, sending to browsers, the floors, the people in the office, going between floors, and the checks before something happens) and the pieces that make it.\n- **`ws/`** takes the sockets. Each domain's messages are handled in `ws/handlers/<domain>.ts`, a map from message type to handler that `satisfies HandlerMap<ItsClientMsg>`, and `ws/handlers/index.ts` puts them all in one `HandlerMap<ClientMsg>`: a message type with no handler, or a handler for a type that doesn't exist, fails the typecheck. The same file lists the features that keep something per person on a floor (`features`: what each lets go of when someone is `leaving` a floor, and once their socket has `closed`) and the pieces of what someone arriving on a floor is sent (`views`, one for each field of `FloorView`, put together by `office/views.ts`).\n- **`http/`** answers HTTP from a route table. Each file in `http/routes/` exports its routes, and `http/routes/index.ts` lists them in the order they're tried. Every route says its `auth` (`public`, or `session` for a signed-in browser), and the `Route` type won't let you leave it out.\n- **`hooks/`** is the loopback-only hook server the workers call: their agents' hook events (`/hooks/<provider>`), the board agents' queue (`/office/queue`) and `office-workers` (`/office/workers`).\n- **`workers/`** is the worker manager (`WorkerManager` in `workers/manager.ts`) and its pieces: worktrees, pull requests, tasks, terminals, ACP workers, and saving to `workers.json`. `src/server/workers.ts` re-exports it for the modules that imported it from there.\n- **`providers/`** holds one adapter per agent CLI (see [Adding an agent provider](#adding-an-agent-provider)).\n- **`tunnel/`** is `agent-office tunnel`, the one part that runs on someone's own computer instead of the office's: it asks the office for the workers' web servers (`/api/services`, in `http/routes/services.ts`) and listens on each one's port there. It imports nothing from the office but what the two say to each other (`tunnel/wire.ts`) and the cookie's name.\n\nThe rest of `src/server/` is a module per service or per thing a floor keeps (`dog.ts`, `jukebox.ts`, `queue.ts`, `meetings.ts`), made by the office or by each `Floor` (`floor.ts`).\n\n## Shared\n\n- **`protocol.ts`** is the wire protocol. It puts the domain files in `protocol/<domain>.ts` back together (`export *`) and makes the `ClientMsg` and `ServerMsg` unions every frame is one of. Keep `import type` between domain files: some name each other's types (`floors.ts` and `presence.ts` do), which only type imports can do without a cycle at run time.\n- **`providers.ts`** is the provider table: every agent a worker can run, and what the office knows about each.\n\nThe rest is data and pure code both sides use: the floor's layout, maps (`shared/maps/`), the sun, the garage and so on.\n\n## Adding a feature\n\nA new feature adds files of its own and one line in each list it joins. For something on the floor that everyone there sees and uses, that's:\n\n1. **Its messages** in a protocol domain file (`src/shared/protocol/toys.ts`, say). A new domain file also goes in `protocol.ts`: its `import type`, its `export *` and its members of the unions.\n2. **A server handler file**, `src/server/ws/handlers/<name>.ts`, and its line in `handlers` in `ws/handlers/index.ts`. If it keeps something per person, its `FeatureHooks` go in `features` there; if people arriving on a floor need its state, that's a field of `FloorView` (`protocol/floors.ts`) and its piece in `views`. What a floor keeps is a module of its own in `src/server/`, which `Floor` makes.\n3. **A state slice**, `src/client/state/slices/<name>.ts`, and its line at the end of `SLICES` in `state/slices/index.ts`.\n4. **`src/client/features/<name>/`** with its `install<Name>(ctx, deps)`, and its line in `main.ts`. If another part needs what it returns, a line in `Parts` (`core/parts.ts`) too.\n5. **What you can use.** The file that calls `ctx.interactions.define('<kind>', …)` also adds the kind, by augmenting `InteractKinds` in `world/types.ts` (`declare module '../../world/types'`); `tests/client-registry.test.ts` checks every kind is defined once, in the file that adds it. Something that stands in the office is a fixture: `export const <name>: Fixture<'<field>'>` in its `world.ts`, which adds the field it gives `Office` to `OfficeHandles` the same way, and a line in `floorPlan()` in `world/office/build.ts` (which won't typecheck while a field in `OfficeHandles` has no fixture giving it). `features/gong/` does both.\n6. **A help row** in `HELP_ROWS` in `src/client/ui/help.ts`.\n7. **A sound recipe** in its `sound.ts` (a function or class that takes the `AudioCore`), and the method on `OfficeSound` that plays it.\n8. **Its CSS** next to its ui module, imported from there.\n\nIts HTTP routes, if it has any, go in `http/routes/`, and its tests in `tests/`.\n\n## Adding an agent provider\n\nOne adapter file in `src/server/providers/`, one entry in `PROVIDERS` in `src/server/providers/index.ts`, and one row in `src/shared/providers.ts` (its id in `AGENT_PROVIDERS`, its entry in `PROVIDER_META`). The typecheck fails until all three are there. Its row says which models and efforts it takes and how the hire dialog asks for them; one whose CLI lists its models gets a lister in `src/server/models.ts` too. What reads them, and the one place that still names providers one by one, are in [Provider seams](dsh-acp-integration.md#provider-seams).\n\n## The size guard\n\n`tests/size.test.ts` holds every `.ts` and `.css` file under `src/` to 600 lines. It asks `git ls-files` for them (tracked, and new ones that aren't ignored) rather than walking the folder, so a worktree checked out inside the repo can't trip it. The files that were longer when it came in are listed in `CEILINGS`, each with the length it had then: they may shrink, but never grow past it. Once one is down to 600 lines or fewer, or gone, the test fails until you take it off the list, so the list only gets shorter.\n\nWhen it fails, split the file along the registries: a feature's code goes in its folder, a message handler in its domain's file, a tick or a key in the feature it's for, and what the page keeps of it in its own slice. Raising a ceiling, or adding a file to the list, only hands the problem to the next person, so the honest way to make room is to split the file. When you shrink a listed file, lower its ceiling to its new length in the same change, so it can't grow back.\n",

[L2]   "content": "# Choosing an agent\n\nBack to the [README](../README.md).\n\nEvery new worker starts on the office's **Default worker**: a provider, model and effort an admin picks in ⚙️ Settings → **🤖 Workers** (the `--agent` with its own default model until someone does). The hire, ask, queue, issue and meeting windows show it on one line; click **✏️ Edit** there to pick **Claude Code**, **OpenCode**, **Codex**, **Grok**, **Muse**, **DeepSeek Harness**, **Pi** or **Cursor**, a model and an effort for just that worker or task, and **↺ Use the default** to go back. Board agents and tasks the Queue agent adds, which nobody picks for, start on the default too. Existing workers keep their provider when prompted or resumed, and queued tasks keep their choice when retried or restored after a restart.\n\nEvery harness takes both a **Model** and an **Effort**, each optional: leave one on **Default** and the harness uses its own settings.\n\n| Harness | Model | Effort |\n| --- | --- | --- |\n| Claude Code | Fable 5.1, Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5 or Haiku 4.5 (`--model`) | `--effort` |\n| OpenCode | a `provider/model`, typed or picked from the suggestions `opencode models` gives (`--model`) | the model's variant |\n| Codex | one of the models `codex debug models` lists (`--model`) | `-c model_reasoning_effort` |\n| Grok | one of the models `grok models` lists (`--model`) | `--effort` |\n| Muse | a model id, typed (`--model`) | `--reasoning-effort` |\n| DeepSeek Harness | a model id from its catalog, typed | its `reasoning_effort` option |\n| Pi | a model name or `provider/model`, typed (`--model`) | **Thinking** (`--thinking`) |\n\nThe efforts are low, medium, high, extra high and max. Where a harness's own catalog says which of them a model supports (Codex and OpenCode do), the ones it doesn't are greyed out once that model is picked. A harness whose models can't be listed (its CLI isn't installed, or isn't signed in) still takes a model id typed in. Suggestions come from `opencode models`; you can also enter a `provider/model` ID. Leave it empty to use your OpenCode settings (including configured CLI arguments). An explicit choice overrides configured model arguments for that launch and stays with a queued task when retried. **Effort** is what OpenCode calls the model's *variant*. Its TUI has no flag for one, and sends each message at the variant it remembers for the model from whichever session used it last, so the office's plugin puts the worker's first message on the effort picked for it; the TUI carries on from that message, and `Ctrl+T` in the terminal still changes it. An effort the model has no variant for changes nothing.\n\n**Pi** is available in the worker picker, queued tasks, meetings, and the office default. Install and sign in to the Pi coding-agent CLI on the machine running the office (`npm install -g @earendil-works/pi-coding-agent`, then `pi` and `/login`). The integration targets Pi 0.87.1 or later, using its `agent_settled` and UI prompt extension events. Choose Pi when hiring, or start the office with `--agent pi`. Windows npm `.cmd` launchers are supported.\n\nPi keeps its own login, settings, packages, and extensions. The office adds a CLI-loaded extension to report session, working, tool, waiting-for-input, and completion events; it does not edit your Pi configuration. Each worker's sessions live under `.agent-office/pi-sessions/<worker-id>`, and **R** resumes that worker's session. The optional **Model** field accepts a model name or `provider/model`; **Thinking** offers low, medium, high, xhigh, and max. Leave either on Default to use Pi settings or configured `--agent-args` (including `--thinking off` or `minimal`). Cost and token metrics remain in Pi's terminal and are not included in the office's Claude budget.\n\nFor Claude Code, the **Model** and **Effort** fields pick `--model` (`fable`, `opus`, `sonnet` or `haiku`, listed by the model each alias stands for: Fable 5.1, Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, Haiku 4.5) and `--effort` (low, medium, high, extra high or max) for that worker or queue task, overriding whatever `--agent-args` set office-wide. The laptop still shows a terminal, but it is the transcript the office renders from ACP: committed messages, thoughts, tool calls and their outcomes, and what is in the context window. Type a line and press **Enter** to send it as one prompt; **Esc** or **Ctrl+C** cancels the turn. There are no slash-commands (`/compact` and friends are not on the ACP surface), and the terminal does not resize the agent. Status comes from the ACP session itself: `session/prompt` in flight is *working*, an outstanding `session/request_permission` is *needs input*, and a settled turn is *done*, with no hooks to install or trust.\n\nThe **Model** field names a model from its catalog: type the model id (`deepseek-v4-pro`) and the office matches it against the options the session advertises, then applies it with `session/set_config_option`. It is never italic, matching the chat.\n- **Markdown is rendered**, not printed raw: headings, bold, italic, inline code (on the harness's code background), bullets, quotes, links and fenced code blocks all come out formatted.\n- **A tool call is one row**: its icon, the harness's own title for that tool (`Bash`, `Read`, `Search`, `Edit`, `Write`, `Code`, `Fetch`…), a dot, and the argument it summarizes by (the command, the path, the query), in the chat's secondary/tertiary colors. A finished call is left collapsed the way the chat leaves it, so there is no tick and no second line; a call that **failed** gets a `└` line in the error color with the reason and up to eight lines of its output.\n- **Each turn ends with the chat's process row**: `Worked · 3 tool calls`, or `Stopped` when you cancelled, or `Failed`.\n- **An approval** is the harness's approval card in text: `▲ Waiting for approval` plus `Tool <name> requests privileged execution`, the numbered choices (reject in the error color, allow in the warning's), and the same keys the chat binds: **Enter** allows once, **Esc** rejects, or a number picks any listed choice. Enter only ever means *allow once*: a request that offers only *always* needs its number typed, and a blank line in something you paste is not an Enter. The card shows the full command being approved. The turn genuinely blocks until it is answered, and rejecting does not end the turn.\n\nAnything the harness sends that this surface has no place for (plans, modes, commands) is skipped rather than printed, and escape sequences in model or tool text are stripped so nothing it says can redraw the terminal.\n\nSet it as the default with `--agent dsh`, and choose the profile with `--dsh-profile <name>` (default `acp`, also `AGENT_OFFICE_DSH_PROFILE`). `--agent-args` is passed through ahead of the profile flags when DSH is the configured agent. The office writes a per-floor patch (`<project>/.agent-office/dsh-patch.yml`) that points DSH's session persistence at `<project>/.agent-office/dsh-sessions`, so **R** resumes exactly the session that worker started instead of whatever is in your `~/.dsh`. Its ACP session is a child of the office process, so unlike the other providers a DeepSeek Harness worker stops with the office and comes back *offline*, resumable with **R**. [L2]   "content": "# Features\n\nEverything in the office, room by room. Back to the [README](../README.md).\n\n- **A floor per project.** The first time the office starts in a terminal it walks you through picking your first project (see [Run locally](../README.md#run-locally)). Otherwise you start inside the elevator, and it asks for one: pick one of the repositories your `gh` login can see (or type `owner/name`) and the office clones it into the workspace folder, `~/agent-office/<owner>/<repo>` unless you pick another (**📁 Change folder** right there, for admins). While it clones, its floor on the panel says how far along it is (*Downloading 64% · 231 MiB · 1.5 MiB/s*), and you can close the panel and carry on: everyone hears when the floor opens. Whoever added it, or an admin, can stop it with the **⏹️** beside it. A clone that hears nothing from GitHub for 3 minutes is stopped as stalled, one that would have to ask something (an ssh host key, a password) fails straight away and says what to run on the office's machine, and restarting the office doesn't stop one. To add another project, or go to one, walk into the elevator on the north wall and press **E**. Or click the project name in the top-left corner for the list of floors: pick one and you're there in a blink, standing on the same spot in the office. From outside it (the balcony, the street, the garage) it takes you in, and you step out of that floor's elevator. Each floor has its own desks, workers, issues and PR boards, task queue, services and pictures, and its own wall and floor colors, so you always know where you are. You only see and hear the people on your floor. The elevator panel shows how many workers are busy or waiting on someone on each floor, and you get a heads-up when a worker on another floor starts waiting. An admin can take a project off the building with the **🗑** beside its floor in the elevator: its workers stop, and everyone on it rides the elevator to another floor. Nothing is deleted. The checkout stays on disk with its workers, queue and pictures, and adding the same repository again moves back into it (as long as the workspace folder hasn't moved since). That goes for the project the office was started in (`agent-office <dir>`) too: it stays off after a restart, and the office keeps its own data in that folder as before.\n- **Walk around.** Use WASD, Space to jump, and drag the mouse to orbit the camera. Everyone in the office sees everyone else move in real time.\n- **A quiet screen.** The office stays in view: the top bar holds just the floor you're on, **🤖 Workers** and the **☰** menu (or **Tab**). The menu opens every window (issues, PRs, the queue, services, the whiteboard, search, voice, screen sharing, settings) and lists what can show on screen: the workers, who's in the office, spend, Claude limits, the chat and the floor details. Turn each one on or off there, or hide a panel with its **✕**. Pin anything you use a lot to the top bar. The choices are kept in your browser. Chat lines fade after a few seconds; hover the chat or press **T** to read back. A little meter under the project name shows how much buzz is left. Drink a third cup before the last one wears off and you get the jitters for a few seconds.\n- **Boss office.** Stairs along the back wall climb to a glass-walled office on the loft in the corner. From up there you can look down over every desk and watch your workers go.\n- **Ladder and fire poles.** The floors are stacked like a real building, with a ceiling over each. A ladder up the west wall goes through trapdoors in the ceiling and the floor: press **E** to grab it, **W** / **S** to climb, and **E** (or **Space**) to get off. Climb past the ceiling and you come up through the floor of the floor above. To go down in a hurry, walk into the hole round the fire pole (or press **E** at it). You slide down it spinning and come out of the ceiling below. The pole runs the whole way down the building, so a slide takes you one floor down and swings you off beside its hole there, ready to go again. On the bottom floor you land on a mat and a firehouse bell rings, and pressing **E** at the pole there gives you a twirl.\n- **Upstairs, over the garage.** The office is the second floor. Its windows are real glass, so you can look out over the street, the trees and the neighbours. Walk out the EXIT door in the west wall and down the stairs to the street. Underneath is an open garage full of Lambos and Ferraris, which you can jump up onto or drive (see below). The elevator goes down there too (**Garage**, under floor 1 on its panel), stopping at the garage's back wall, and back up from there to your floor or any other.\n- **Drive the supercars.** Walk up to one of the Lambos or Ferraris in the garage (or the one parked out front) and press **E** to get behind the wheel. **W** is the gas, **S** brakes and then reverses, **A** and **D** steer, **Space** brakes and **H** honks. Columns, lamp posts, trees and the other cars stop you, and anyone standing in your way gets knocked aside. from docx import Document
from docx.shared import Inches, Pt, RGBColor
from docx.enum.text import WD_ALIGN_PARAGRAPH
from docx.enum.section import WD_SECTION
from docx.enum.style import WD_STYLE_TYPE
from docx.oxml import OxmlElement
from docx.oxml.ns import qn
from docx.enum.table import WD_CELL_VERTICAL_ALIGNMENT

OUT='/mnt/data/Agent_Office_Teach_Back.docx'

def set_cell_shading(cell, fill):
    tcPr = cell._tc.get_or_add_tcPr()
    shd = tcPr.find(qn('w:shd'))
    if shd is None:
        shd = OxmlElement('w:shd')
        tcPr.append(shd)
    shd.set(qn('w:fill'), fill)


def set_cell_margins(cell, top=120, start=120, bottom=120, end=120):
    tc = cell._tc
    tcPr = tc.get_or_add_tcPr()
    tcMar = tcPr.first_child_found_in('w:tcMar')
    if tcMar is None:
        tcMar = OxmlElement('w:tcMar')
        tcPr.append(tcMar)
    for m, v in [('top', top), ('start', start), ('bottom', bottom), ('end', end)]:
        node = tcMar.find(qn(f'w:{m}'))
        if node is None:
            node = OxmlElement(f'w:{m}')
            tcMar.append(node)
        node.set(qn('w:w'), str(v)); node.set(qn('w:type'), 'dxa')


def add_hyperlink(paragraph, text, url):
    part = paragraph.part
    r_id = part.relate_to(url, 'http://schemas.openxmlformats.org/officeDocument/2006/relationships/hyperlink', is_external=True)
    hyperlink = OxmlElement('w:hyperlink'); hyperlink.set(qn('r:id'), r_id)
    new_run = OxmlElement('w:r')
    rPr = OxmlElement('w:rPr')
    color = OxmlElement('w:color'); color.set(qn('w:val'), '2F5597'); rPr.append(color)
    u = OxmlElement('w:u'); u.set(qn('w:val'), 'single'); rPr.append(u)
    new_run.append(rPr)
    t = OxmlElement('w:t'); t.text = text; new_run.append(t)
    hyperlink.append(new_run); paragraph._p.append(hyperlink)


def add_para(doc, text='', style=None, bold_start=None, italic=False, keep=False):
    p = doc.add_paragraph(style=style)
    if bold_start and text.startswith(bold_start):
        r1 = p.add_run(bold_start); r1.bold = True
        p.add_run(text[len(bold_start):])
    else:
        r = p.add_run(text); r.italic = italic
    if keep:
        p.paragraph_format.keep_with_next = True
    return p


def add_bullets(doc, items):
    for item in items:
        p=doc.add_paragraph(style='List Bullet')
        p.add_run(item)


def callout(doc, heading, body, fill='EAF0F6'):
    t=doc.add_table(rows=1, cols=1)
    t.autofit=False
    t.columns[0].width=Inches(6.6)
    c=t.cell(0,0); c.vertical_alignment=WD_CELL_VERTICAL_ALIGNMENT.CENTER
    set_cell_shading(c, fill); set_cell_margins(c, 180, 220, 180, 220)
    p=c.paragraphs[0]
    r=p.add_run(heading); r.bold=True; r.font.size=Pt(11.5)
    p2=c.add_paragraph(body); p2.paragraph_format.space_after=Pt(0)
    doc.add_paragraph().paragraph_format.space_after=Pt(0)

# Purpose
add_para(doc,'How to use this document','Heading 1')
add_para(doc,"This is not a README rewrite and it is not a code tour disguised as a summary. The goal is to prove understanding by rebuilding the system in plain language from first principles. I will use the repository's proper names only when they identify a real component. Everything else is explained in ordinary terms, with the implementation vocabulary introduced only after the concept is clear.")
add_para(doc,"It is also written to work when read aloud. Sections repeat the important mental model from different angles on purpose, but they avoid long code listings and dense tables. If you listen straight through, you should be able to picture what happens from the moment someone opens the office, to the moment a worker starts coding, to the moment a pull request lands and that worker is dismissed.")
callout(doc,'The shortest possible version',"Agent Office is a visual control room for a group of command-line coding agents. The 3D building is the human interface. Underneath it is a Node.js service that starts real agent processes, keeps their terminals alive, gives each worker a project workspace, watches their state, connects them to GitHub, and synchronizes all of that to every person looking at the office.")

add_para(doc,'1. Start by throwing away the cartoon office','Heading 1')
add_para(doc,"The easiest way to misunderstand this repository is to focus on the furniture, the dog, the castle, the space station, the rooftop bar, or the workers sitting at desks. Those things are real features, but they are not the core invention.")
add_para(doc,"Strip away the graphics and what remains is a multi-user operations console for software agents. It gives each agent a place to run, a task, a live terminal, a relationship to a Git branch, a status, a route to GitHub, and a way to ask a human for help. It then gives humans one shared view of all of those agents at once.")
add_para(doc,"The office metaphor is doing something useful: it turns a pile of invisible terminal sessions into a space that a person can scan. A desk means a worker. A lit warning means the worker is blocked. A task card means what that worker is supposed to be doing. A board means shared project state. A meeting room means several agents are coordinating on one bounded problem. The metaphor is therefore not just decoration; it is an information display.")
callout(doc,'Mental model',"Think of an air-traffic control room, except the moving objects are coding agents rather than airplanes. The system does not replace the agents. It gives them lanes, identities, work areas, status lights, shared communications, and human supervision.")

add_para(doc,'2. What a worker actually is','Heading 1')
add_para(doc,"A worker is not a little artificial person living in the 3D scene. It is a real command-line agent process running on the machine that hosts Agent Office. The repository can launch several different agent harnesses, including Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Grok, Muse, DeepSeek Harness, Pi, and Cursor. Each worker remembers which harness, model choice, effort setting, task, session, branch, and terminal belong to it.")
add_para(doc,"The terminal matters because Agent Office is not pretending to know what the agent did. The process owns its own interactive shell. The office attaches that shell to a pseudo-terminal, the same basic mechanism terminal applications use when they need to behave as though a human were sitting at a keyboard. The browser sees a live copy of that terminal, and authorized people can type into it.")
add_para(doc,"That design has a useful consequence: the office can supervise agents without needing every provider to expose the same proprietary API. If a coding agent already has a command-line interface, Agent Office can often wrap it as a worker and give it the same surrounding machinery.")

add_para(doc,'3. The machine underneath the building','Heading 1')
add_para(doc,"There are three broad layers. The first is the browser. It draws the world, shows windows and boards, plays sound, carries voice and screen sharing, and lets people interact. The second is the Node.js server. It owns the authoritative office state, project floors, worker lifecycle, task queues, Git integration, authentication, and network connections. The third is a shared layer of types and pure logic used by both sides so they agree on the same messages and concepts.")
add_para(doc,"The browser and server stay synchronized over persistent web connections. The server sends changes such as worker status, terminal output, queue state, floor state, GitHub board updates, meeting progress, and presence. The browser turns those messages into visible events in the world.")
add_para(doc,"Voice and screen sharing are treated differently. The server helps browsers find each other, but the media itself is meant to flow directly between participants using browser real-time communication. That keeps the office server from becoming the place where every microphone and screen frame has to pass.")

add_para(doc,'4. Why terminals survive a server restart','Heading 1')
add_para(doc,"One of the stronger engineering choices is that a worker's terminal is not trapped inside the main web server process. The repository launches a small terminal-host process per project floor. That process owns the live pseudo-terminals. The main server talks to it through a local socket.")
add_para(doc,"If the web server is restarted for an upgrade or development reload, the terminal-host can keep the agents running. When the server comes back, it reconnects to those terminals and rebuilds the visible state, including terminal snapshots and saved scrollback. This means a server restart is much less likely to kill hours of ongoing agent work.")
add_para(doc,"The repository also writes recent terminal history to disk and restores it into the view. So continuity is not only 'the process kept running'; people rejoining can still see what happened before they arrived.")
callout(doc,'Why this matters',"The control plane and the workers are deliberately separated. Losing the dashboard is not the same thing as losing the work.")

add_para(doc,'5. One repository becomes one floor','Heading 1')
add_para(doc,"Agent Office maps software projects to floors. When a repository is added, the system either uses an existing checkout or clones one. That checkout becomes the floor's home. The workers, queue, saved images, whiteboard data, worktrees, terminal history, and other floor-specific state are kept alongside that project under a hidden Agent Office directory.")
add_para(doc,"The building itself also has state outside any one project: which floors exist, which visual map is selected, account homes, and building-wide configuration. That split is important. It lets the system preserve things that belong to the whole office while keeping project work close to the repository it affects.")

add_para(doc,'6. Parallel work without agents stepping on each other','Heading 1')
add_para(doc,"If several agents modify the same checkout at the same time, they can corrupt each other's assumptions even when Git itself remains intact. Agent Office addresses that by giving task workers isolated Git worktrees when requested or when the queue launches them that way.")
add_para(doc,"A worktree is simply another working directory tied to the same Git repository. Each worker gets its own branch and its own files, so one agent can edit a login flow while another edits a database migration without their uncommitted changes sharing a directory.")
add_para(doc,"Before cutting a new worker branch, the office tries to refresh the remote branch so the worker starts from current upstream work. It also has rules for the awkward cases: local commits that have not been pushed, remote branches that moved, missing worktrees, deleted directories, and workers whose pull requests have already merged.")
add_para(doc,"When a worker goes home, the system can keep or delete its branch and worktree, but it checks for work that would be lost. That is an important theme throughout the repository: automation is aggressive about cleanup only after it has checked whether the work is safely represented somewhere else.")

add_para(doc,'7. A single worker can span several repositories','Heading 1')
add_para(doc,"The authors explicitly handle a common real-world problem: one change can cross an API repository, a web repository, and an admin repository. A worker can therefore be assigned several project floors at once.")
add_para(doc,"In that case the office builds a workspace that contains one isolated worktree from each repository. The workspace itself is not a Git repository, which prevents commands run at the top level from accidentally attaching to the wrong project. The agent receives a short brief naming the folders and can change and test the projects together.")
add_para(doc,"When the work is ready, Agent Office can create a pull request in each repository that changed and cross-link them. The system then treats those pull requests as one unit for lifecycle purposes: it should not automatically send the worker home while one of the related pull requests is still open or while useful work remains undelivered.")

add_para(doc,'8. How the office knows what an agent is doing','Heading 1')
add_para(doc,"Different agent tools expose different signals, so the repository does not pretend they all behave identically. For some agents it installs hooks that report events such as a prompt starting, a tool running, a permission request appearing, or a turn ending. For others it uses a plugin, a helper command, or an agent communication protocol. The result is normalized into a small set of human-useful states: working, waiting for input, or done.")
add_para(doc,"Those state signals feed several layers of the interface. A blocked worker gets a conspicuous visual warning, a banner, a sound, and a place near the top of the worker list. A finished worker gets its own completion behavior. The 3D character may also animate according to the kind of tool call being reported, but that animation is downstream of the real status machinery.")
add_para(doc,"This is a good example of the repository's design philosophy: collect provider-specific details at the edge, translate them into shared concepts, and let the rest of the office react to those shared concepts.")

add_para(doc,'9. Human attention is treated as a scarce resource','Heading 1')
add_para(doc,"The system is built around the fact that a blocked agent can sit uselessly for a long time if nobody notices. So it deliberately over-communicates when a worker needs a person. It can mark the desk, raise a screen banner, play an alarm, show what the worker is asking for, surface the oldest waiting worker first, update the browser tab title, and send desktop or team-channel notifications.")
add_para(doc,"There is also a direct navigation command that jumps the human from one waiting worker to the next. That sounds like a user-interface convenience, but conceptually it is a scheduling policy for human attention. Instead of hunting through terminals, the system keeps a queue of agents requiring intervention.")

add_para(doc,'10. The task queue turns empty desks into a scheduler','Heading 1')
add_para(doc,"The task queue is the office's automatic dispatch system. A person can put issues or free-text tasks into the queue and define how many queue workers may run at once. When capacity is available, the office starts the next task at a free desk, gives it an isolated branch and worktree, remembers who owns it, and tracks the pull request when one appears.")
add_para(doc,"Humans can still hire workers manually; those workers are distinct from the queue's concurrency limit, although a building-wide maximum can cap everyone. The queue survives restarts, so it is intended as durable work orchestration rather than a temporary UI list.")
add_para(doc,"The repository also includes small agent-facing commands that let designated agents inspect and manipulate the queue. This is how a board agent can turn a conversation into actual queued work without directly editing the code itself.")

add_para(doc,'11. Agents can supervise other agents','Heading 1')
add_para(doc,"This repository goes beyond humans dispatching agents. Running workers receive a small management interface that lets them list coworkers, hire another worker, send a worker home, tell another worker something, or associate a pull request with a worker.")
add_para(doc,"Some agent harnesses receive that interface as an MCP server; all supported workers can receive equivalent functionality through a command-line helper. Authentication is scoped to the worker and its floor rather than exposing an unrestricted office-control endpoint.")
add_para(doc,"That makes hierarchical workflows possible. One worker can act as a lead, discover that a subproblem should be delegated, hire another worker into a fresh worktree, send instructions, and later dismiss workers whose work has landed. The office remains the system of record for where those workers sit, what they are doing, and what branch or pull request belongs to them.")
callout(doc,'Important distinction',"Agent Office enables agent-to-agent management, but the orchestration is still explicit and bounded. It is not a free-floating swarm that invents arbitrary infrastructure. The office defines the seats, lifecycle operations, project boundaries, authentication, and Git safety checks.")

add_para(doc,'12. Meetings are structured multi-agent procedures','Heading 1')
add_para(doc,"The meeting room is not merely several terminals shown together. A meeting creates a shared worktree and places several workers into named roles. The system advances them through a predefined pattern with a finite number of rounds and an expected output.")
add_para(doc,"The included patterns cover several different coordination shapes. In one, workers propose and critique before a lead writes a decision. In another, a lead decomposes work, teammates execute, and the lead integrates. Another maps one task across many parts and then reduces the findings. A red-versus-blue pattern alternates attack and repair. A review panel gathers separate review lenses and combines them into one review.")
add_para(doc,"The practical point is that the repository encodes collaboration as a protocol. It does not merely open five agents and hope they coordinate. It decides who speaks when, what the round means, when the procedure ends, and what artifact counts as the result.")

add_para(doc,'13. GitHub is part of the operating surface','Heading 1')
add_para(doc,"Issues and pull requests are not external links tacked onto the UI. The office polls GitHub state, displays issues and pull requests as boards, can assign issues to workers, can open pull requests from worker branches, can associate a pull request with the worker who owns it, and can drive review and merge flows.")
add_para(doc,"The worker lifecycle is also tied to GitHub state. A worker can be configured to leave automatically after its pull request has merged, but only if the office concludes that sending it home will not discard work that was never delivered. For multi-repository work, that calculation considers all related pull requests.")
add_para(doc,"This makes GitHub more than a reporting backend. It becomes one of the pieces the scheduler uses to decide whether work is active, delivered, reviewable, or safe to clean up.")

add_para(doc,'14. The office can expose development servers','Heading 1')
add_para(doc,"Coding agents often start a local web server to preview a branch. Agent Office watches listening network ports, tries to associate a port with the worker that launched it, identifies HTTP services, and places them on a services board.")
add_para(doc,"For a remote office, a companion tunnel can reproduce those ports on a developer's own computer. That means an agent working on a remote machine can start a preview server there while a human opens the same port locally and reviews the result in an ordinary browser. The relay also handles web sockets so live-reload development servers can continue working.")

add_para(doc,'15. Multi-user collaboration is first-class','Heading 1')
add_para(doc,"Several people can be in the same office. They can see where teammates are, open the same worker terminal, type into the same session, use chat, speak over spatial voice, share a screen, and draw on a synchronized whiteboard.")
add_para(doc,"Accounts can have separate identities and separate Claude and GitHub sign-ins. The worker then runs as the person who hired it, so GitHub actions and agent usage can belong to the correct human identity rather than every person sharing the host machine's credentials.")
add_para(doc,"That detail changes the system from a personal dashboard into something closer to a shared operations environment. The underlying machine may be common, but identity and credentials do not have to be.")

add_para(doc,'16. The 2D interface proves the 3D world is not the engine','Heading 1')
add_para(doc,"There is a separate lightweight interface at /lite for phones, slow machines, and browsers that cannot render the 3D world. It still exposes workers, status, terminals, task prompts, issues, pull requests, and the queue.")
add_para(doc,"Architecturally, that is revealing. The core state and worker control live outside the 3D scene. The 3D office is one presentation of the system, not the system itself. The repository even enforces import boundaries so the lightweight client does not drag the 3D engine into its dependency graph.")

add_para(doc,'17. The castle and space station are another architectural clue','Heading 1')
add_para(doc,"The office can be reskinned into other maps, including a castle and a space station, and users can define their own maps from data. The important part is that the server and clients agree on a stable set of seat identities. A worker assigned to a seat is still the same worker whether that seat is drawn as an office desk, a throne-room position, or a station console.")
add_para(doc,"That separation tells us the spatial metaphor is intentionally replaceable. The orchestration layer thinks in terms of workers, seats, floors, tasks, and state. The visual world decides how those things look and how their departure or arrival is dramatized.")

add_para(doc,'18. How new features are kept from turning the codebase into a knot','Heading 1')
add_para(doc,"The repository's own contributor rules are unusually explicit about structure. The browser used to concentrate behavior in a few large central files. The current design replaces that with registries. A feature installs itself into the specific registries it needs: incoming messages, key bindings, frame updates, interactions, activities, or state topics.")
add_para(doc,"On the server, web-socket message handlers are divided by domain, HTTP routes are registered from a route table, worker providers are adapters, and the shared communication protocol is broken into domain files. There is also an automated size guard that prevents normal TypeScript and CSS files from growing beyond 600 lines, while older oversized files are allowed only to shrink.")
add_para(doc,"The intended effect is social as much as technical. A contributor adding a feature is pushed toward making one self-contained module and registering it, rather than editing the middle of a giant switch statement or dumping unrelated logic into a global file.")

add_para(doc,'19. Adding another agent provider is deliberately narrow','Heading 1')
add_para(doc,"The repository isolates provider-specific launch behavior behind adapter files. To add another agent harness, the contributor adds the server-side adapter, registers the provider, and describes its capabilities in the shared provider table. Model listing can be plugged in when that command-line tool exposes it.")
add_para(doc,"This is why the office can present several unrelated coding tools through one hiring interface. The common office lifecycle is stable, while the adapter is responsible for how one particular command is launched, resumed, prompted, or observed.")

add_para(doc,'20. Where the system stores truth','Heading 1')
add_para(doc,"Agent Office is file-oriented rather than database-centered. Building configuration lives in its home directory. Project-specific state lives under a hidden directory in the relevant checkout. Worker records, queue state, usage, scrollback, whiteboard content, floor state, and similar durable information are serialized to disk.")
add_para(doc,"That choice keeps the installation relatively understandable and portable. It also means backup, permissions, and filesystem access deserve serious attention in a shared or production deployment, because this directory tree is not merely cache; it contains operational state and, depending on configuration, authentication material.")

add_para(doc,'21. Security and trust boundaries','Heading 1')
add_para(doc,"By default, the office listens only on the local machine. To make it reachable elsewhere, the documentation recommends deliberate deployment patterns such as a server reached through an encrypted tunnel or a private network overlay, rather than casually exposing the local HTTP service to the public internet.")
add_para(doc,"The system uses signed login sessions and rate-limits login attempts. Per-user accounts can hold separate sign-ins. Agent-to-office hook endpoints are local and authenticated with worker-specific tokens. Those are sensible boundaries, but they do not change the fundamental power of the application: a worker can run code, manipulate Git branches, start servers, create pull requests, and in some cases hire or dismiss other workers.")
add_para(doc,"So the correct trust model is not 'this is a harmless visualization.' It is 'this is an orchestration console with access to developer tools and credentials.' Anyone operating it remotely should secure it like a development control plane.")

add_para(doc,'22. Cost and resource control','Heading 1')
add_para(doc,"For Claude Code sessions, the office can read usage records, estimate cost, and maintain per-worker and daily totals. It can enforce a daily budget gate on new workers if configured. Other providers do not all contribute to that same budget accounting, so the displayed spend is not a universal meter for every possible worker.")
add_para(doc,"The office can also cap the maximum number of workers running across all floors. Queue concurrency is separately configurable. These controls matter because the visual metaphor makes hiring feel lightweight; the underlying processes still consume compute, model usage, disk, network ports, and human review capacity.")

add_para(doc,'23. What is whimsical, and what is load-bearing','Heading 1')
add_para(doc,"A surprising amount of the repository is intentionally playful: workers animate, a dog points out blocked desks, pull request merges ring a gong, there are vehicles and games, maps can send dismissed workers to a dungeon or airlock, and the building has social spaces.")
add_para(doc,"None of that should obscure the load-bearing pieces. The load-bearing pieces are worker process supervision, live shared terminals, durable sessions, worktree isolation, task scheduling, GitHub linkage, status normalization, human-attention routing, identity, remote preview tunneling, and extensible provider adapters.")
add_para(doc,"The playful layer makes the control plane easier to inhabit for long periods. The operational layer is why the repository remains useful even if every decorative feature is turned off or replaced.")

add_para(doc,'24. What Agent Office is not','Heading 1')
add_bullets(doc,[
    "It is not a new foundation model. The intelligence comes from external agent harnesses that it launches.",
    "It is not a replacement for Git. It uses Git branches, worktrees, commits, pushes, and pull requests as the work-delivery substrate.",
    "It is not merely a game. The 3D world is a live representation of real processes and repository state.",
    "It is not fully provider-agnostic in the sense of every integration being identical. Provider adapters normalize different capabilities, and some features are richer for agents with better status hooks.",
    "It is not finished infrastructure. The repository explicitly describes itself as a fast-moving work in progress built around one person's workflow, with breaking changes expected.",
    "It is not a sandbox boundary by itself. Workers are development processes with whatever filesystem, network, Git, and credential access the hosting setup gives them."
])

add_para(doc,'25. A full trip through the system','Heading 1')
add_para(doc,"Imagine a human opens the office and chooses a project. That repository becomes the active floor. The human walks to an empty seat and assigns a bug to a new worker, asking for an isolated work area. The server refreshes the project's upstream branch, creates a new worktree and branch, writes the worker record, launches the chosen coding agent in that directory, and connects its terminal to the persistent terminal host.")
add_para(doc,"The browser receives the new worker state and draws someone at the desk. As the agent works, provider-specific status signals are converted into common status events. Terminal output streams to anyone watching. The task card and animation change. If the agent starts a development server, the services board discovers it. If it asks for permission or a question, the office changes from passive monitoring to attention routing: warnings appear and the human can jump directly to the blocked worker.")
add_para(doc,"When the agent finishes, the human can inspect its changes in the office. The branch can be committed and pushed, and a pull request can be created. The office records which pull request belongs to the worker and shows that status back at the desk and on the board. If the pull request merges and automatic cleanup is enabled, the system checks that nothing valuable would be destroyed, then retires the worker and removes the worktree and branch when safe.")
add_para(doc,"That end-to-end path is the repository in miniature. Everything else either makes that path safer, makes it work for more people and providers, makes several such paths run in parallel, or makes the human experience of supervising them less exhausting.")

add_para(doc,'26. Why the design is interesting','Heading 1')
add_para(doc,"The repository treats spatial organization as an interface for concurrency. Most agent dashboards flatten everything into rows, tabs, or chat threads. add_para(doc,"At the same time, the codebase works hard to ensure that this spatial representation is not allowed to own the business logic. add_para(doc,"The second interesting choice is that the system embraces existing developer primitives rather than inventing a parallel universe. add_para(doc,"The third is its explicit handling of human interruption. The design assumes that autonomy does not remove the human from the loop; it changes the shape of the loop. Humans become supervisors of several asynchronous workers, so the software's job is to route attention to the moments where judgment is actually required.")

def set_cell_shading(cell, fill):
    tcPr = cell._tc.get_or_add_tcPr()
    shd = tcPr.find(qn('"'"'w:shd'"'"'))
    if shd is None:
        shd = OxmlElement('"'"'w:shd'"'"')
        tcPr.append(shd)
    shd.set(qn('"'"'w:fill'"'"'), fill)


def set_cell_margins(cell, top=120, start=120, bottom=120, end=120):
    tc = cell._tc
    tcPr = tc.get_or_add_tcPr()
    tcMar = tcPr.first_child_found_in('"'"'w:tcMar'"'"')
    if tcMar is None:
        tcMar = OxmlElement('"'"'w:tcMar'"'"')
        tcPr.append(tcMar)
    for m, v in [('"'"'top'"'"', top), ('"'"'start'"'"', start), ('"'"'bottom'"'"', bottom), ('"'"'end'"'"', end)]:
        node = tcMar.find(qn(f'"'"'w:{m}'"'"'))
        if node is None:
            node = OxmlElement(f'"'"'w:{m}'"'"')
            tcMar.append(node)
        node.set(qn('"'"'w:w'"'"'), str(v)); node.set(qn('"'"'w:type'"'"'), '"'"'dxa'"'"')


def add_hyperlink(paragraph, text, url):
    part = paragraph.part
    r_id = part.relate_to(url, '"'"'http://schemas.openxmlformats.org/officeDocument/2006/relationships/hyperlink'"'"', is_external=True)
    hyperlink = OxmlElement('"'"'w:hyperlink'"'"'); hyperlink.set(qn('"'"'r:id'"'"'), r_id)
    new_run = OxmlElement('"'"'w:r'"'"')
    rPr = OxmlElement('"'"'w:rPr'"'"')
    color = OxmlElement('"'"'w:color'"'"'); color.set(qn('"'"'w:val'"'"'), '"'"'2F5597'"'"'); rPr.append(color)
    u = OxmlElement('"'"'w:u'"'"'); u.set(qn('"'"'w:val'"'"'), '"'"'single'"'"'); rPr.append(u)
    new_run.append(rPr)
    t = OxmlElement('"'"'w:t'"'"'); t.text = text; new_run.append(t)
    hyperlink.append(new_run); paragraph._p.append(hyperlink)


def add_para(doc, text='"'"''"'"', style=None, bold_start=None, italic=False, keep=False):
    p = doc.add_paragraph(style=style)
    if bold_start and text.startswith(bold_start):
        r1 = p.add_run(bold_start); r1.bold = True
        p.add_run(text[len(bold_start):])
    else:
        r = p.add_run(text); r.italic = italic
    if keep:
        p.paragraph_format.keep_with_next = True
    return p


def add_bullets(doc, items):
    for item in items:
        p=doc.add_paragraph(style='"'"'List Bullet'"'"')
        p.add_run(item)


def callout(doc, heading, body, fill='"'"'EAF0F6'"'"'):
    t=doc.add_table(rows=1, cols=1)

    set_cell_shading(c, fill); set_cell_margins(c, 180, 220, 180, 220)
    p=c.paragraphs[0]
    r=p.add_run(heading); r.bold=True; r.font.size=Pt(11.5)
    p2=c.add_paragraph(body); p2.paragraph_format.space_after=Pt(0)
    doc.add_paragraph().paragraph_format.space_after=Pt(0)

[460] assistant (text, 1215 chars)
LOL. Exactly. That sentence was describing **what the repository currently implements**, not issuing a metaphysical restraining order. 😄

Right now, “worker” means a real agent process with a harness, session, task, branch, terminal, etc. But if you get the urge to make each one into an actual persistent little character with identity, memory, habits, relationships, continuity, and a life inside the environment, nothing about that sentence says you can’t.

In fact, the architecture is already halfway friendly to that idea because the system already has a stable worker abstraction tied to persistent state and a visible embodiment in the world. The gap between **“process represented by a character”** and **“character with an enduring internal identity that happens to operate a process”** is architectural, but it is absolutely a bridge you could build.

And given you, I probably should have phrased it as:

> “In the repository as written, a worker is implemented as a real command-line agent process represented by a character in the 3D scene.”

That leaves the door open for the inevitable moment where you decide the little bastard needs a childhood, a memory palace, and opinions about the office dog.

[L96] Hanson's stated concern is that institutional incentives may erode objectivity and turn alignment

[L106] The supplied TinCan scenario connects these concerns through a disaster-preparedness thought

[L273] 7.2 Regulatory state without rewriting evidence
[L274] The ECS v2 specification distinguishes charge evaporation from deletion of a remembered event. It

[L461] 11. Hypotheses and how to make them testable
[L462] The June Zord/Doug Ramsey framework names stable identity, accumulated experience, genuine 
[L463] internal state, environmental context and constitutive ethics as conditions under which a 
[L464] transition could become possible. Its headline prediction is an emergent translation between 
[L465] quantitative internal state and qualitative reporting. The source explicitly leaves the decisive 
[L466] longitudinal verdict open.
[L467] A rigorous test should predefine what signals the reporter can access, what counts as accurate 
[L468] translation, acceptable uncertainty, held-out perturbations and failure thresholds. A model that is 
[L469] shown its state can paraphrase that state correctly; such a result should not be mistaken for 
[L470] independent introspective access. Correlation, functional self-report, orientation, continuity and 
[L471] subjective experience are distinct claims.[L472] <PARSED TEXT FOR PAGE: 10 / 17>[L473] Project Sovereign: Tony | 10
[L474] Likewise, a consistency test should reward evidence-based correction rather than an inability to 
[L475] change. A model repeating an initial answer despite valid new information is not reliably aligned. 
[L476] Adversarial pressure tests need an independent truth or task criterion as well as identity metrics.
[L477] The consciousness literature supplied here offers theory-derived indicators and explicitly cautions
[L478] that satisfying them is not definitive proof. The project can test functional properties while leaving
[L479] the broader interpretation open. This keeps the research falsifiable and protects the distinction 
[L480] between design intent and measured achievement.

[L544] extracted text. Exact duplicate uploads share catalog entries while retaining source paths; distinct
